claim: The Global Typhoid Genomics Consortium was established to bring together the typhoid research community to aggregate and analyse Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (Typhi) genomic data to inform public health action.
source: The Global Typhoid Genomics Consortium was established to bring together the typhoid research community to aggregate and analyse Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (Typhi) genomic data to inform public health action.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the purpose of the consortium.

claim: This analysis represents the largest Typhi genome sequence collection to date (n=13,000).
source: This analysis, which marks 22 years since the publication of the first Typhi genome, represents the largest Typhi genome sequence collection to date (n=13,000).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this is the largest collection with 13,000 genomes.

claim: Genotype 4.3.1 (H58) has not spread beyond Asia and Eastern/Southern Africa.
source: Compared with previous global snapshots, the data highlight that genotype 4.3.1 (H58) has not spread beyond Asia and Eastern/Southern Africa
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: In regions outside Asia and Eastern/Southern Africa, distinct genotypes dominate and have independently evolved AMR.
source: in other regions, distinct genotypes dominate and have independently evolved AMR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility (>1 resistance determinant) is widespread across geographies and genotypes.
source: The data indicate that ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility (>1 resistance determinant) is widespread across geographies and genotypes
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: High-level ciprofloxacin resistance (≥3 determinants) has reached 20% prevalence in South Asia.
source: with high-level ciprofloxacin resistance (≥3 determinants) reaching 20% prevalence in South Asia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid has become dominant in Pakistan (70% in 2020) but has not yet become established elsewhere.
source: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid has become dominant in Pakistan (70% in 2020) but has not yet become established elsewhere.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ceftriaxone resistance has emerged in eight non-XDR genotypes, including a ciprofloxacin-resistant lineage (4.3.1.2.1) in India.
source: Ceftriaxone resistance has emerged in eight non-XDR genotypes, including a ciprofloxacin-resistant lineage (4.3.1.2.1) in India.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in Table 3.

claim: Azithromycin resistance mutations were detected at low prevalence in South Asia, including in two common ciprofloxacin-resistant genotypes.
source: Azithromycin resistance mutations were detected at low prevalence in South Asia, including in two common ciprofloxacin-resistant genotypes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Typhoid fever was responsible for an estimated 10.9 million illnesses and 116,800 deaths worldwide in 2017.
source: but was still responsible for an estimated 10.9 million illnesses and 116,800 deaths worldwide in 2017, largely in parts of the world where WASH is suboptimal (GBD 2017 Typhoid and Paratyphoid Collaborators, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the GBD 2017 study.

claim: Mortality ratios for typhoid fever are estimated <1% today, but in the pre-antibiotic era ranged from 10% to 20%.
source: mortality ratios are estimated <1% today, but in the pre-antibiotic era ranged from 10% to 20% (Andrews et al., 2018; Stuart and Pullen, 1946).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the mortality estimates.

claim: Multidrug resistance (MDR) in typhoid emerged in the 1970s.
source: but multidrug resistance (MDR, defined as combined resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and co-trimoxazole) emerged in the 1970s
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citations.

claim: The first completed whole genome sequence of Typhi was published in 2001.
source: In 2001, the first completed whole genome sequence of Typhi was published (Parkhill et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the Parkhill et al. 2001 paper.

claim: The sequenced isolate CT18 was an MDR isolate cultured from a typhoid fever patient in the Mekong Delta region of Vietnam in 1993.
source: The sequenced isolate was CT18, an MDR isolate cultured from a typhoid fever patient in the Mekong Delta region of Vietnam in 1993.
evidence: This is stated as background information about the first sequenced Typhi genome.

claim: Typhi evolves at a rate of approximately 0.5 substitutions per year.
source: Typhi evolves on the order of 0.5 substitutions per year, much more slowly than host-generalist Salmonella, such as S. enterica serovars Kentucky and Agona (five substitutions per year) (Achtman et al., 2021; Duchêne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the evolutionary rate estimate.

claim: The GenoTyphi framework was developed based on an analysis of almost 2000 Typhi isolates from 63 countries.
source: The GenoTyphi scheme was initially developed based on an analysis of almost 2000 Typhi isolates from 63 countries (Wong et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the Wong et al. 2016a paper.

claim: The GenoTyphi framework defined 4 primary clades, 15 clades, and 49 subclades using 68 marker SNVs.
source: This dataset was used to define a global population framework based on 68 marker SNVs, which were used to define 4 primary clades, 15 clades, and 49 subclades organised into a pseudo-hierarchical framework.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the GenoTyphi framework.

claim: H58 (genotype 4.3.1) was strongly associated with AMR and was found throughout Asia as well as Eastern and Southern Africa.
source: H58 (genotype 4.3.1) was strongly associated with AMR and was found throughout Asia as well as Eastern and Southern Africa (Wong et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the Wong et al. 2016a paper.

claim: The genetic basis for MDR was a conjugative plasmid of incompatibility type IncHI1.
source: The genetic basis for MDR was a conjugative (i.e. self-transmissible) plasmid of incompatibility type IncHI1 (Anderson, 1975)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Anderson 1975.

claim: The IncHI1 plasmid accumulated genes (blaTEM-1, cat, dfr, and sul) encoding resistance to all three first-line drugs.
source: This plasmid accumulated genes (blaTEM-1, cat, dfr, and sul) encoding resistance to all three first-line drugs, mobilised by nested transposons (Tn6029 in Tn21, in Tn9) (Holt et al., 2011b; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the genetic basis of MDR.

claim: H58 is estimated to have originated in South Asia in the mid-1980s.
source: which is estimated to have originated in South Asia in the mid-1980s (Carey et al., 2022; da Silva et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the origin estimate.

claim: H58 spread throughout South East Asia and into Eastern and Southern Africa.
source: before spreading throughout South East Asia (Holt et al., 2011a; Pham Thanh et al., 2016b) and into Eastern and Southern Africa (Feasey et al., 2015; Kariuki et al., 2010; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the spread of H58.

claim: Ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility is mainly caused by substitutions in the quinolone resistance determining region (QRDR) of core chromosomal genes gyrA and parC.
source: The genetic basis for this is mainly substitutions in the quinolone resistance determining region (QRDR) of core chromosomal genes gyrA and parC, which directly impact fluoroquinolone binding.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism for ciprofloxacin non-susceptibility.

claim: A single QRDR mutation (typically at gyrA codon 83 or 87) results in a moderate increase in ciprofloxacin MIC to 0.06–0.25 mg/L.
source: The most common genetic pattern is a single QRDR mutation (typically at gyrA codon 83 or 87), which results in a moderate increase in ciprofloxacin MIC to 0.06–0.25 mg/L (Day et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the MIC range.

claim: An accumulation of three QRDR mutations raises ciprofloxacin MIC to 8–32 mg/L.
source: An accumulation of three QRDR mutations raises ciprofloxacin MIC to 8–32 mg/L and is associated with higher occurrence of clinical failure (Pham Thanh et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the MIC range.

claim: The XDR clone of Typhi (genotype 4.3.1.1.P1) was first reported in late 2016 in Hyderabad, Pakistan.
source: Reports of ceftriaxone treatment failure in late 2016 in Hyderabad, Pakistan, led to the discovery of an extensively drug-resistant (XDR, defined as MDR plus resistance to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins) clone of Typhi (genotype 4.3.1.1.P1, a subtype of H58), which subsequently spread throughout Pakistan (Klemm et al., 2018; Rasheed et al., 2020; Yousafzai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the discovery of XDR Typhi.

claim: The XDR clone 4.3.1.1.P1 harbours a common combination of chromosomal AMR determinants (integrated MDR transposon plus single QRDR mutation, GyrA-83) and has acquired an IncY-type plasmid carrying resistance genes, including qnrS and blaCTX-M-15.
source: This XDR clone harbours a common combination of chromosomal AMR determinants (integrated MDR transposon plus single QRDR mutation, GyrA-83) but has also acquired an IncY-type plasmid carrying resistance genes, including qnrS (which, combined with GyrA-83 results in a ciprofloxacin-resistant [CipR] phenotype with MIC >1 mg/L) and the extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) encoded by blaCTX-M-15 (Klemm et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the genetic characterization of XDR Typhi.

claim: Azithromycin-resistant (AziR) Typhi is associated with mutations in the chromosomal gene acrB.
source: Azithromycin-resistant (AziR) Typhi, which is associated with mutations in the chromosomal gene acrB, has now been reported across South Asia (Carey et al., 2021; Duy et al., 2020; Iqbal et al., 2020; Sajib et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the genetic basis of azithromycin resistance.

claim: A total of 13,000 confirmed Typhi genomes were collated from 65 studies and 5 unpublished public health laboratory datasets.
source: A total of 13,000 confirmed Typhi genomes were collated from 65 studies and 5 unpublished public health laboratory datasets (see Table 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the data collection.

claim: N=35 genomes had assembly sizes outside of the plausible range (4.5–5.5 Mbp), leaving n=12,965 high-quality genomes originating from 110 countries.
source: N=35 genomes had assembly sizes outside of the plausible range (4.5–5.5 Mbp, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), leaving n=12,965 high-quality genomes originating from 110 countries.
evidence: This is stated as a quality control step in the data processing.

claim: The majority of genomes originated from Southern Asia (n=8231), specifically India (n=2705), Bangladesh (n=2268), Pakistan (n=1810), and Nepal (n=1436).
source: The majority originated from Southern Asia (n=8231), specifically India (n=2705), Bangladesh (n=2268), Pakistan (n=1810), and Nepal (n=1436).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the geographical distribution of genomes.

claim: H58 lineage (4.3.1 and derived genotypes) is the dominant form of Typhi in Southern Asia with an overall prevalence of 70.4% [95% CI, 69.3–71.5%].
source: The genotype distribution confirms the widely reported finding that the H58 lineage (4.3.1 and derived genotypes) is the dominant form of Typhi in Southern Asia, where it is thought to have originated (Carey et al., 2022; Roumagnac et al., 2006; da Silva et al., 2022; Wirth, 2015; Wong et al., 2015) (overall prevalence, 70.4% [95% CI, 69.3–71.5%]; n=4662/6623).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data.

claim: In Bangladesh, H58 was associated with a minority of genomes (42% [n=670/1591]), compared with 73% in India, 74% in Nepal, and 94% in Pakistan.
source: Notably though, the distribution of H58 genotypes was different between countries in the region (see Figure 1b), and in Bangladesh, it was associated with a minority of genomes (42% [n=670/1591], compared with 73% in India [n=1655/2267], 74% in Nepal [n=941/1275], and 94% in Pakistan [n=1390/1484]).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data for each country.

claim: In Pakistan, lineage 1 (genotype 4.3.1.1 and derived genotypes) was most common (73%; 1089/1484), with the XDR sublineage (genotype 4.3.1.1.P1) appearing in 2016 and rapidly rising to dominance (87% in 2020).
source: In Pakistan, lineage 1 (genotype 4.3.1.1 and derived genotypes) was most common (73%; 1089/1484), with the XDR sublineage (genotype 4.3.1.1.P1) appearing in 2016 (Gul et al., 2017; Klemm et al., 2018; Rasheed et al., 2020) and rapidly rising to dominance (87% in 2020 [n=27/31]; see Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data in Figure 1b.

claim: In South-eastern Asia, H58 accounted for 47.3% [95% CI, 43.2–51.3%; 276/584] of isolates in aggregate (mostly 4.3.1.1, 43.0% of total genomes; 251/584).
source: In South-eastern Asia, H58 accounted for 47.3% [95% CI, 43.2–51.3%; 276/584] of isolates in aggregate (mostly 4.3.1.1, 43.0% of total genomes; 251/584).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data.

claim: H58 accounted for nearly all isolates in Cambodia (98%, n=216/221, all lineage 1), Myanmar (94%, n=46/49, mixed lineages), and Singapore (n=4/4, mixed lineages), but was largely absent from Indonesia (3%, n=2/65), Laos (4%, n=1/27), and the Philippines (0.5%, n=1/206).
source: However, the population structures varied between individual countries in the region (see Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with H58 accounting for nearly all isolates in Cambodia (98%, n=216/221, all lineage 1), Myanmar (94%, n=46/49, mixed lineages), and Singapore (n=4/4, mixed lineages), but largely absent from Indonesia (3%, n=2/65), Laos (4%, n=1/27), and the Philippines (0.5%, n=1/206).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data for each country.

claim: H58 was the dominant cause of typhoid in Eastern Africa during the study period (93.3% H58 [95% CI, 91.5–95.0%] n=774/830).
source: Our aggregated data confirmed that H58 was the dominant cause of typhoid in Eastern Africa during the study period (93.3% H58 [95% CI, 91.5–95.0%] n=774/830; see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data.

claim: At the region level in Eastern Africa, 4.3.1.1.EA1 dominated (78%, [95% CI 75.1–80.8%] n=647/830).
source: Here, we found that at the region level, 4.3.1.1.EA1 dominated (78%, [95% CI 75.1–80.8%] n=647/830; see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data.

source: In Western Africa, the common genotypes were 3.1.1 (64.4%, [95% CI, 58.7–70.2%]; n=172/266) and 2.3.2 (13.9%, [95% CI, 9.7–18.0%] n=37/266) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data.

claim: Central American isolates were dominated by 2.3.2 (55%, [95% CI, 45.2–64.8%] n=55/100), which was also common in Western Africa (13.9%, [95% CI, 9.7–18.0%]; n=37/266).
source: Strikingly, Central American isolates were dominated by 2.3.2 (55%, [95% CI, 45.2–64.8%] n=55/100), which was also common in Western Africa (13.9%, [95% CI, 9.7–18.0%]; n=37/266) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data.

claim: CipNS is emerging or established in all regions except Melanesia.
source: Our data demonstrate that CipNS is emerging or established in all regions except Melanesia (here represented by n=35 genomes from Fiji and Papua New Guinea, mainly from 2010, although more recent reports support a lack of CipNS in Fiji [Davies et al., 2022; Getahun Strobel et al., 2019]; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CipNS was emerging or established in all countries with sufficient data to assess (≥50 genomes) except Ghana.
source: For countries with sufficient data to assess (≥50 genomes), CipNS was emerging or established in all countries except Ghana (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: CipR typhoid is now a well-established problem across Southern Asia and is emergent in Chile, Mexico, and South Africa.
source: Notably, the data suggest that CipR typhoid is now a well-established problem across Southern Asia and is emergent in Chile, Mexico, and South Africa (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: A total of 26 distinct CipR genotypes (comprising unique combinations of Typhi genotype, QRDR mutations, and/or PMQR genes) were identified.
source: A total of 26 distinct CipR genotypes (comprising unique combinations of Typhi genotype, QRDR mutations, and/or PMQR genes) were identified, of which five were found in appreciable numbers (>5 genomes each, see Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: The XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 was first identified in Pakistan in 2016 and accounted for 75% of Typhi genomes from Pakistan in 2020.
source: The XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 (carrying GyrA-S83F+qnrS) was first identified in Pakistan in 2016 (Klemm et al., 2018; Rasheed et al., 2020), and here accounted for 75% of Typhi genomes from Pakistan in 2020 and a dramatic rise in CipR prevalence (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The CipR strain 4.3.1.3.Bdq (carrying GyrA-S83F and qnrS) emerged in Bangladesh in ~1989 and accounted for 95% of CipR genomes in this country.
source: The CipR strain 4.3.1.3.Bdq (carrying GyrA-S83F and qnrS) emerged in Bangladesh in ~1989 (da Silva et al., 2022) and here accounted for 95% of CipR genomes in this country.
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by data.

claim: Most Indian CipR genomes belong to 4.3.1.2.1 (92.3%).
source: Most Indian CipR genomes belong to 4.3.1.2.1 (92.3%).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: CipR 4.3.1.2.1 was also found in 12 other countries, most notably Nepal, Pakistan, Myanmar, and Chile.
source: CipR 4.3.1.2.1 was also found in 12 other countries, most notably Nepal (accounting for 95% of CipR genomes), where it has been shown to have been introduced from India and result in treatment failure (Pham Thanh et al., 2016a); Pakistan (accounting for 6.6% of CipR genomes); Myanmar (accounting for n=17/17 CipR genomes); and Chile (accounting for n=5/5 CipR genomes) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: MDR prevalence has declined in India (p=2 × 10–9 using proportion trend test) to 2% (0–3% per year, 2016–2020).
source: Prevalence of MDR (co-resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and co-trimoxazole) has declined in India (p=2 × 10–9 using proportion trend test) to 2% (0–3% per year, 2016–2020), and is similarly rare in Nepal (mean 5% in 2011–2019) (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: MDR prevalence has also declined in Bangladesh (p=2 × 10–4 using proportion trend test) but remains high enough to discourage deployment of older first-line drugs, with prevalence exceeding 20% in most years.
source: MDR prevalence has also declined in Bangladesh (p=2 × 10–4 using proportion trend test) but remains high enough to discourage deployment of older first-line drugs, with prevalence exceeding 20% in most years (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: In Pakistan, the emergence of the XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 has driven up MDR prevalence dramatically (p=4 × 10–11 using proportion trend test), to 87% in 2020.
source: In Pakistan, the emergence of the XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 has driven up MDR prevalence dramatically (p=4 × 10–11 using proportion trend test), to 87% in 2020 (see Figure 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: MDR prevalence has remained high in Kenya and Malawi since the first arrival of MDR H58 strains (estimated early 1990s in Kenya; 2009 in Malawi).
source: MDR prevalence has remained high in Kenya and Malawi since the first arrival of MDR H58 strains (estimated early 1990s in Kenya [Kariuki et al., 2021]; 2009 in Malawi [Feasey et al., 2015])
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the timing of MDR arrival.

claim: MDR prevalence has declined steadily in Nigeria, from 72% in 2009 to 10% in 2017 (p=3 × 10–4 using proportion trend test).
source: but has declined steadily in Nigeria, from 72% in 2009 to 10% in 2017 (p=3 × 10–4 using proportion trend test; see Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: All MDR isolates in Nigeria were genotype 3.1.1 and carried large IncHI1 MDR plasmids.
source: All MDR isolates in Nigeria were genotype 3.1.1 and carried large IncHI1 MDR plasmids, which are associated with a fitness cost (Doyle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the fitness cost.

claim: Chromosomal integration of the MDR transposon accounted for 100% of MDR in Malawi and 19% in Kenya (all in H58 genotype backgrounds).
source: Chromosomal integration of the MDR transposon, which accounted for 100% of MDR in Malawi and 19% in Kenya (all in H58 genotype backgrounds), is associated with comparably lower fitness cost
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The genome of strain Rwp1-PK1, isolated from Rawalpindi in July 2015, was identified as genotype 4.3.1.1.P1.
source: Here, we identified the genome of strain Rwp1-PK1 (assembly accession NIFP01000000), isolated from Rawalpindi in July 2015, as genotype 4.3.1.1.P1.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Rwp1-PK1 was isolated from a 17-year-old male with symptomatic typhoid whose infection did not resolve following ceftriaxone treatment and was found to be phenotypically XDR.
source: Rwp1-PK1 was isolated from a 17-year-old male with symptomatic typhoid whose infection did not resolve following ceftriaxone treatment and was found to be phenotypically XDR (resistant to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, chloramphenicol, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone) (Munir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original report.

claim: The Rwp1-PK1 genome carries the 4.3.1.1.P1 marker SNV, clusters with the 4.3.1.1.P1 sublineage in a core-genome tree, and shares the full set of AMR determinants typical of 4.3.1.1.P1.
source: We found that the Rwp1-PK1 genome carries the 4.3.1.1.P1 marker SNV, clusters with the 4.3.1.1.P1 sublineage in a core-genome tree (Figure 4), and shares the full set of AMR determinants typical of 4.3.1.1.P1
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 4 showing the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: This XDR strain was present in northern Pakistan for at least a full year before it was reported as causing outbreaks in the southern province of Sindh.
source: indicating that this XDR strain was present in northern Pakistan for at least a full year before it was reported as causing outbreaks in the southern province of Sindh.
evidence: This is inferred from the isolation date of Rwp1-PK1 (July 2015) compared to the first reports of XDR outbreaks in Sindh (late 2016).

claim: ESBL genes were identified in n=32 non-4.3.1.1.P1 genomes, belonging to eight other genotypes.
source: However, ESBL genes were identified in n=32 non-4.3.1.1.P1 genomes, belonging to eight other genotypes (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Table 3 showing the data.

claim: IncY plasmids carrying blaCTX-M-15 were rare (n=1–4 genomes) in all genotype backgrounds except 4.3.1.1.P1 (total n=655).
source: However, overall, blaCTX-M-15 IncY plasmids were rare (n=1–4 genomes) in all genotype backgrounds except 4.3.1.1.P1 (total n=655), suggesting that the IncY blaCTX-M-15 plasmid has not been stably maintained in other Typhi lineages (see Table 3).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Table 3 showing the data.

claim: A sublineage of 4.3.1.2.1 from India carrying blaSHV-12 in a IncX3 plasmid backbone comprised 15 isolates from Mumbai (2015–2018), plus three additional isolates from travellers returning to England, Australia, and the USA from India (2018–2020).
source: This group comprised 15 isolates from Mumbai (Argimón et al., 2021b; Jacob et al., 2021) (across two studies, 2015–2018), plus three additional isolates from travellers returning to England, Australia, and the USA from India (Chattaway et al., 2021; Ingle et al., 2021) (2018–2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the data.

claim: This strain appears to have originated in Mumbai and persisted there since at least 2015 for at least 6 years, but the data do not indicate onward spread out of Maharashtra or India.
source: This strain therefore appears to have originated in Mumbai and persisted there since at least 2015 for at least 6 years, but our data do not indicate onward spread out of Maharashtra or India.
evidence: This is inferred from the geographical and temporal distribution of isolates.

claim: AziR-associated mutations in acrB were identified in 74 genomes.
source: AziR-associated mutations in acrB were identified in 74 genomes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The majority of acrB mutants were from Bangladesh (n=55, 73%), followed by India (n=11, 15%).
source: The majority of acrB mutants were from Bangladesh (n=55, 73%), followed by India (n=11, 15%) (see Figure 5a)
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 5a showing the data.

claim: The overall prevalence of acrB mutations was very low even in Bangladesh (2.6%) and India (0.5%).
source: although the overall prevalence of resistance was very low even in these locations (2.6% in Bangladesh, 0.5% in India).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Thirteen distinct combinations of genotype and acrB mutation were identified, implying at least thirteen independent events of AziR emergence.
source: Thirteen distinct combinations of genotype and acrB mutation were identified, implying at least thirteen independent events of AziR emergence
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of genotype-mutation combinations.

claim: The three more common AziR variants all carried R717Q, in 4.3.1.1 (n=38, mainly from Bangladesh), 3.2.2 (n=12, from Bangladesh), or 4.3.1.2 (n=7, from India).
source: The three more common AziR variants all carried R717Q, in 4.3.1.1 (n=38, mainly from Bangladesh), 3.2.2 (n=12, from Bangladesh), or 4.3.1.2 (n=7, from India).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Half (n=7/13) of all acrB/genotype combinations were identified in Bangladesh.
source: Notably, half (n=7/13) of all acrB/genotype combinations were identified in Bangladesh (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 4b showing the data.

claim: All acrB mutants also carried QRDR mutations, and eight were cipR.
source: All acrB mutants also carried QRDR mutations, and eight were cipR
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Six acrB mutants belong to the CipR 4.3.1.2.1 lineage in India (all carried R717Q and were isolated in 2017 in Chandigarh).
source: n=6 belong to the CipR 4.3.1.2.1 lineage in India (all carried R717Q and were isolated in 2017 in Chandigarh)
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Two acrB mutants belong to the CipR 4.3.1.3.Bdq lineage (both carried R717L and were isolated in 2019, one in Singapore and one in Bangladesh).
source: and n=2 belong to the CipR 4.3.1.3.Bdq lineage (both carried R717L and were isolated in 2019, one in Singapore and one in Bangladesh).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In most cases (67% of genotype-source combinations), genotype prevalence rates estimated from individual source laboratories yielded 95% CIs that overlapped with those of the pooled national estimates.
source: In most cases (67% of genotype-source combinations), genotype prevalence rates estimated from individual source laboratories yielded 95% CIs that overlapped with those of the pooled national estimates (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing the data.

claim: The main exception was for genotype 4.3.1.2 in India; for most source laboratories, this was the most prevalent genotype, but the point estimates ranged from 16% to 82%, compared with the pooled estimate of 53.4% (95% CI, 51.4–55.5%).
source: The main exception was for genotype 4.3.1.2 in India; for most source laboratories (many contributing via the Surveillance for Enteric Fever in India [SEFI] network; Carey et al., 2020; da Silva et al., 2022), this was the most prevalent genotype, but the point estimates ranged from 16% to 82%, compared with the pooled estimate of 53.4% (95% CI, 51.4–55.5%), and 95% CIs were frequently non-overlapping (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated with citations and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing the data.

claim: High prevalence of 4.3.1.2 was estimated from contributing laboratories in urban Vellore (82% [95% CI, 78–87%]), Chennai (67% [56–77%]), Bengaluru (70% [62–78%]), and Mumbai (two laboratories, estimates 74% [65–83%] and 63% [46–79%]).
source: High prevalence of 4.3.1.2 was estimated from contributing laboratories in urban Vellore (82% [95% CI, 78–87%]), Chennai (67% [56–77%]), Bengaluru (70% [62–78%]), and Mumbai (two laboratories, estimates 74% [65–83%] and 63% [46–79%])
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence estimates and confidence intervals.

claim: Lower prevalence of 4.3.1.2 was found in northern India, New Delhi (three laboratories, estimates 48% [28–68%], 40% [31–49%], 39% [22–56%]) and Chandigarh (39% [33–45%]).
source: with lower prevalence in northern India, New Delhi (three laboratories, estimates 48% [28–68%], 40% [31–49%], 39% [22–56%]) and Chandigarh (39% [33–45%]).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence estimates and confidence intervals.

claim: Two Indian laboratories were clear outliers, with little or no 4.3.1.2 but very high prevalence of a different genotype: 4.3.1.1 in rural Bathalapalli (81% [67–95%]) and 2.5 in the northern city of Ludhiana (77% [66–88%]).
source: Two Indian laboratories were clear outliers, with little or no 4.3.1.2 but very high prevalence of a different genotype: 4.3.1.1 in rural Bathalapalli (81% [67–95%]) and 2.5 in the northern city of Ludhiana (77% [66–88%]).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence estimates and confidence intervals.

claim: AMR prevalence estimates were highly concordant across data sources.
source: AMR prevalence estimates were also highly concordant across data sources (see Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and showed strikingly similar temporal trends (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: For Nigeria, genotype prevalence estimates were concordant across different sources, with single-laboratory 95% CIs overlapping with one another and with the pooled point estimate, for all five common genotypes.
source: Genotype prevalence estimates were concordant across different sources, with single-laboratory 95% CIs overlapping with one another and with the pooled point estimate, for all five common genotypes (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 7 showing the data.

claim: The exception for Nigeria was that genotype 3.1.1 accounted for all n=14/14 isolates sequenced from Ibadan, but ranged from 53% to 70% prevalence at other laboratories and yielded a pooled national prevalence estimate of 67% [95% CI, 60–75%].
source: The exception was that genotype 3.1.1 accounted for all n=14/14 isolates sequenced from Ibadan, but ranged from 53% to 70% prevalence at other laboratories and yielded a pooled national prevalence estimate of 67% [95% CI, 60–75%] (see Figure 7a and c).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 7 showing the data.

claim: AMR prevalence estimates for Nigeria were more variable across laboratories, but this could be explained by their non-overlapping sampling times.
source: AMR prevalence estimates for Nigeria were more variable across laboratories (see Figure 7b), but this could be explained by their non-overlapping sampling times
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 7b showing the data.

claim: Abuja data from earlier years (2010–2013) showed high MDR (49%) and low CipNS (4%); whereas Ibadan data from later years (2017–2018) showed comparatively lower MDR (21%) and higher CipNS (79%).
source: Abuja data from earlier years (2010–2013) showed high MDR (49%) and low CipNS (4%); whereas Ibadan data from later years (2017–2018) showed comparatively lower MDR (21%) and higher CipNS (79%), in agreement with contemporaneous travel data (12% MDR, 60% CipNS, from total n=25 isolated 2015–2019).
evidence: This is stated with specific prevalence data for different time periods.

claim: The study has important limitations, most notably the scarcity of genomic data from many countries and world regions where typhoid is believed to be endemic, including Northern and Middle Africa, Western Asia, as well as Central and South America.
source: The study therefore has important limitations, most notably the scarcity of genomic data from many countries and world regions where typhoid is believed to be endemic (GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022), including Northern and Middle Africa, Western Asia, as well as Central and South America (Figures 1—3, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: These genomic data gaps reflect an underlying lack of routine blood culture or sustained blood-culture surveillance, and limited resources and expertise in many settings.
source: These genomic data gaps reflect an underlying lack of routine blood culture or sustained blood-culture surveillance, and limited resources and expertise in many settings (Ikhimiukor et al., 2022b; Iskandar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the explanation for data gaps.

claim: Routine sequencing of travel-associated Typhi infections diagnosed in high-income countries helps to fill some molecular surveillance gaps for some regions.
source: For now, routine sequencing of travel-associated Typhi infections diagnosed in high-income countries helps to fill some molecular surveillance gaps for some regions, assuming that accurate travel history is available and the sequence and metadata (including country of origin) are shared (Ingle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the utility of travel-associated data.

claim: For some countries and regions, travel data represented most or all of the available genome data.
source: Indeed, for some countries and regions, travel data represented most or all of the available genome data (see Table 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated with reference to tables showing the data.

claim: Where multiple data sources were available for the same country, national genotype and AMR prevalence estimates for the period 2010–2020 were largely concordant between local surveillance studies and travel-associated cases captured elsewhere.
source: In this study, where multiple data sources were available for the same country, we found that national genotype and AMR prevalence estimates for the period 2010–2020 were largely concordant between local surveillance studies and travel-associated cases captured elsewhere (Figures 6–7, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–2), particularly when comparing contemporaneous annual prevalence estimates (Figures 6 and 7c).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Travel-associated Typhi isolated in low burden countries can be informative for surveillance of some high burden countries.
source: This clearly shows that travel-associated Typhi isolated in low burden countries can be informative for surveillance of some high burden countries
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance of prevalence estimates between local and travel-associated data.

claim: The WHO has prequalified two TCVs and recommended their use in endemic countries, as well as settings where a high prevalence of AMR Typhi has been reported.
source: The WHO has prequalified two TCVs and recommended their use in endemic countries, as well as settings where a high prevalence of AMR Typhi has been reported (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the WHO recommendation.

claim: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has committed funds to support the procurement and distribution of TCVs in typhoid endemic countries.
source: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has committed funds to support the procurement and distribution of TCVs in typhoid endemic countries (Gavi: The Vaccine Alliance, 2023a; Gavi: The Vaccine Alliance, 2023b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Gavi sources.

claim: Five countries have undertaken Gavi-supported national introductions (Pakistan, Liberia, Zimbabwe, Nepal, Malawi) and one country has self-financed a national introduction (Samoa).
source: Five countries have undertaken Gavi-supported national introductions (Pakistan, Liberia, Zimbabwe, Nepal, Malawi) and one country has self-financed a national introduction (Samoa) (Neuzil, 2020; Sikorski, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the TCV introduction information.

claim: In Pakistan and Zimbabwe, TCV introduction was stimulated by the occurrence of AMR Typhi outbreaks in major urban centres.
source: In Pakistan and Zimbabwe, TCV introduction was stimulated by the occurrence of AMR Typhi outbreaks in major urban centres, highlighting that the case for prevention can be stronger when curative therapy is less available.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about TCV introduction drivers.

claim: TCVs have been shown to be highly effective against drug-resistant Typhi.
source: While TCVs have been shown to be highly effective against drug-resistant Typhi (Batool et al., 2021; Yousafzai et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the effectiveness of TCVs.

claim: The WHO recently released its AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) treatment guidelines, which indicate that choice of empiric therapy should be guided by severity of presentation and local risk of fluoroquinolone resistance.
source: The WHO recently released its AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) treatment guidelines (World Health Organization, 2022), which indicate that choice of empiric therapy should be guided by severity of presentation and local risk of fluoroquinolone resistance
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the WHO guidelines.

claim: If there is low risk of fluoroquinolone resistance, oral ciprofloxacin is recommended for both mild and severe cases.
source: if low risk, oral ciprofloxacin is recommended for both mild and severe cases
evidence: This is stated as part of the WHO AWaRe guidelines.

claim: If there is a high risk of fluoroquinolone resistance, oral azithromycin is recommended for mild cases and intravenous ceftriaxone is recommended for severe cases.
source: and if there is a high risk of fluoroquinolone resistance, oral azithromycin is recommended for mild cases and intravenous ceftriaxone is recommended for severe cases.
evidence: This is stated as part of the WHO AWaRe guidelines.

claim: The guidelines do not indicate which prevalence rate of resistance should warrant avoidance of treatment with ciprofloxacin, nor do they indicate where high prevalence rates of resistance might be expected.
source: However, the guidelines do not indicate which prevalence rate of resistance should warrant avoidance of treatment with ciprofloxacin, nor do they indicate where high prevalence rates of resistance might be expected, although it is noted that drug resistance is most prevalent in Asia.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the WHO guidelines.

claim: This study provides an analytical framework for Typhi genomic analysis, based on an open, robust, reproducible data flow and analysis framework leveraging open-access online data analysis platforms.
source: This study provides an analytical framework for Typhi genomic analysis, based on an open, robust, reproducible data flow and analysis framework leveraging open-access online data analysis platforms (Typhi Mykrobe for read-based genotyping [Ingle et al., 2022]; the GHRU pipeline for genome assembly [Underwood, 2020], and Typhi Pathogenwatch for assembly-based genotyping and tree-building [Argimón et al., 2021b]).
evidence: This is stated with citations to the tools used.

claim: All data processing and statistical analysis code, and underlying sequence and metadata, have been made available via GitHub and FigShare.
source: We have made available all data processing and statistical analysis code, and underlying sequence and metadata, via GitHub and FigShare (see Methods).
evidence: This is stated as a description of data availability.

claim: New insights can be gained from aggregated analysis of published data, which were not evident from the individual contributing studies.
source: Notably, this consortium-driven effort shows that new insights can be gained from aggregated analysis of published data, which were not evident from the individual contributing studies
evidence: This is stated as a key finding of the consortium approach.

claim: The XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 existed in Pakistan in 2015, a year earlier than previously reported.
source: for example (i) the XDR strain 4.3.1.1.P1 existed in Pakistan in 2015, a year earlier than previously reported (Figure 4)
evidence: This is stated as a new insight from the aggregated analysis, supported by Figure 4.

claim: The CefR+CipR strain reported in Mumbai has persisted between at least 2015 and 2020 and is now more easily identified as 4.3.1.2.1 with blaSHV-12.
source: (ii) the CefR+CipR strain reported in Mumbai (Argimón et al., 2021b; Jacob et al., 2021) has persisted between at least 2015 and 2020 and is now more easily identified as 4.3.1.2.1 with blaSHV-12
evidence: This is stated as a new insight from the aggregated analysis, with citations.

claim: Persistence of MDR in certain settings is correlated with migration of MDR from plasmid to chromosome.
source: (iii) persistence of MDR in certain settings is correlated with migration of MDR from plasmid to chromosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which has implications for the future persistence and potentially spread of ESBL strains.
evidence: This is stated as a new insight from the aggregated analysis, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: This dataset provides clear, actionable information about the distribution and temporal trends in AMR across multiple countries and regions.
source: This dataset provides clear, actionable information about the distribution and temporal trends in AMR across multiple countries and regions.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: These data can and should inform prioritisation of TCV introduction and improvements to WASH infrastructure.
source: These data can and should inform prioritisation of TCV introduction and improvements to WASH infrastructure.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Sustaining and expanding genomic surveillance can facilitate measuring the impact of TCV introduction on local bacterial populations.
source: Sustaining and expanding genomic surveillance can also facilitate measuring the impact of TCV introduction on local bacterial populations, as has been done for previous vaccines like pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation with reference to precedent from other vaccines.

claim: Monitoring for potential 'strain replacement' with other Salmonella serovars following TCV introduction can and should inform the prioritisation of the development and deployment of future combination Salmonella vaccines.
source: In addition, monitoring for potential 'strain replacement' with other Salmonella serovars following TCV introduction can and should inform the prioritisation of the development and deployment of future combination Salmonella vaccines.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future surveillance.
